overview.text:
The Ajanta Caves are 30 rock-cut Buddhist caves carved into a horseshoe-shaped cliff above the Waghora river, about 104 km from Chhatrapati Sambhajinagar (Aurangabad). The first were cut in the 2nd and 1st centuries BC and the more richly decorated ones in the Gupta period; their paintings, led by the lotus-holding Padmapani, are counted among the masterpieces of Buddhist art.

The caves were brought to wider attention in 1819 when a shepherd boy led a British officer, John Smith, to Cave 10. Ajanta has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1983. Vehicles stop at Fardapur T-Point, 4 km away, and shuttle buses run to the caves. The site is closed on Mondays; give it its own day apart from Ellora.

overview.text:
The Ellora Caves, near Chhatrapati Sambhajinagar (Aurangabad), are a UNESCO World Heritage Site where Buddhist, Hindu and Jain monks and artisans cut temples and monasteries into the rock between the 6th and 10th centuries. Of more than 100 caves, 34 are open: 12 Buddhist, 17 Hindu and 5 Jain.

The great sight is Cave 16, the Kailasa Temple to Shiva, the largest single monolithic excavation in the world — carved from the top down over more than a century. Cave 10, the Buddhist 'Carpenter's Cave', and the Jain Indra Sabha are close rivals. Stay for the evening light and sound show. Daulatabad Fort is 15 km away and Grishneshwar, the 12th Jyotirlinga, is nearby. Ellora is closed on Tuesdays.
